sourceApproval: Founder-approved under DEC-040 (adapted to Physics Academy rigor)
prerequisites: Lesson 1 — scalars vs. vectors; declare an origin and a positive direction before assigning signs.
Lesson 2 — the slope of a position-time graph is the velocity; read a value off a labelled axis.
majorObjective: Treat velocity as a signed quantity, read and classify segments of a velocity-time graph, decide whether a described motion is constant-velocity using both speed and direction, and calculate signed displacement for a constant-velocity interval with $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t$.
subObjectives: Read a signed velocity value at a stated time from a velocity-time graph.
Classify each segment of a velocity-time graph as constant velocity (horizontal) or changing velocity (sloped), without yet calculating a rate.
State that a negative velocity means motion in the negative direction — not, by itself, that the object is slowing down.
Judge from a description whether velocity is constant, requiring unchanged speed AND unchanged direction.
Calculate signed displacement over a constant-velocity interval using $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t$ with a declared positive direction.

hook.prompt: A car's velocity is $-30\ \mathrm{km/h}$ for a full minute (positive is north). What does the minus sign tell you?
choices: The car is slowing down during that minute.
The car is moving south at a steady $30\ \mathrm{km/h}$.
The car is moving backward relative to how it is pointed.
The car's speedometer would read a negative number.

priorKnowledge: Velocity is a vector: a speed together with a direction. In one dimension the direction is carried entirely by a sign, once a positive direction is declared. Speed is the size of the velocity and is never negative.

chunks.title: Velocity is signed, and a velocity-time graph shows it
chunks.concept:
A **velocity-time graph** plots signed velocity $v$ on the vertical axis against time $t$ on the horizontal axis. Read a velocity the same way you read a position on a position-time graph: go up from the time to the curve, across to the $v$-axis, and keep the sign.

Classify each straight segment by its shape:

- **Horizontal segment** → the velocity is not changing → **constant velocity** over that interval.
- **Sloped segment** → the velocity is changing.

That is all this lesson asks of a sloped segment. *Why* the velocity changes — the rate, the acceleration — is Lesson 5's job. A **negative** velocity value (or a segment below the time axis) means the object is moving in the **negative direction**. It does **not**, on its own, mean the object is slowing down.
chunks.representation:
For each labelled point or segment:

1. Read the velocity value, with its sign.
2. Name the direction the sign means in the declared frame.
3. Classify the segment: horizontal (constant) or sloped (changing).
4. Judge “speeding up / slowing down” only by comparing consecutive speeds — never from the sign alone.

conceptFigures.caption: Segments A (+4 m/s) and B (−4 m/s) and C (+2 m/s) are each horizontal, so velocity is constant within each. The sloped parts (3–4 s and 7–8 s) are intervals of changing velocity.

workedExample.problem: From the graph above, (a) read the velocity on segments A, B, and C, (b) list every constant-velocity interval and every changing-velocity interval, and (c) say whether segment B represents the object slowing down.

phases.label: Read the three segment velocities
steps: Segment A sits on the $+4$ gridline: $v_A = +4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (positive direction).
Segment B sits on the $-4$ gridline: $v_B = -4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (negative direction).
Segment C sits on the $+2$ gridline: $v_C = +2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (positive direction).

phases.label: Judge segment B
steps: Segment B is horizontal, so the velocity is not changing at all during it — the object is neither speeding up nor slowing down there.
The negative sign only says the motion is in the negative direction. “Slowing down” would require the speed to decrease over time, which a horizontal segment never shows.

workedExample.keyMove: Sign is direction; shape (horizontal vs. sloped) is whether the velocity is changing. Read them as two separate facts.

formativeCheck.question: On the velocity-time graph above, which statement about the interval from $t = 4\ \mathrm{s}$ to $t = 7\ \mathrm{s}$ (segment B) is correct?
choices: The object moves at a constant $4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ in the negative direction.
The object is slowing down because the velocity is negative.
The object is at rest because the segment is below the axis.
The object speeds up steadily from $0$ to $4\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

feedback.correct: Correct — the segment is horizontal at $-4\ \mathrm{m/s}$: constant speed of $4\ \mathrm{m/s}$, in the negative direction.

incorrect.1: A negative velocity means “negative direction,” not “slowing down.” The segment is horizontal, so the speed is not changing.
incorrect.2: Below the axis means negative velocity, not zero velocity. At rest would be a horizontal segment sitting exactly on the time axis.
incorrect.3: A steady speed-up would be a sloped segment. This segment is horizontal, so the velocity is unchanging.

hint: The segment is horizontal — so the velocity is not changing. Its height is $-4$, so read that as a direction, not as a trend.
formativeCheck.solution: Segment B is a horizontal line at $v = -4\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Horizontal means constant velocity; the value $-4$ means the motion is in the negative direction at a steady speed of $4\ \mathrm{m/s}$. The sign says nothing about speeding up or slowing down.

chunks.title: Constant velocity needs unchanged speed AND direction
chunks.concept:
**Velocity is constant only when the speed and the direction are both unchanged.** Change either one and the velocity has changed.

The trap is a **reversal**. An object can move at $3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ one way, then $3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ back the other way — the *speed* is $3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ the whole time, but the *velocity* went from $+3$ to $-3\ \mathrm{m/s}$, passing through $0$ during the turn. Equal speed magnitudes before and after a reversal do **not** make the velocity constant.

The same point holds for turning motion: a car going around a bend at a steady $40\ \mathrm{km/h}$ has constant *speed* but changing *velocity*, because its direction keeps changing.
chunks.representation:
To judge a described motion, check two boxes:

1. Is the speed unchanged for the whole interval?
2. Is the direction unchanged for the whole interval?

Only if **both** are yes is the velocity constant. “The speedometer stayed at 40” answers box 1 only — you still need to know whether the direction held.

conceptFigures.caption: Left: velocity holds steady — constant velocity. Right: the speed is 3 m/s before and after, but the velocity swings from +3 to −3 through zero — not constant velocity.

workedExample.problem: On the first graph (segments A, B, C), a student says: “The object's speed is $4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ on segment A and $4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ on segment B, so its velocity is constant from $t = 0$ to $t = 7\ \mathrm{s}$.” Is the student right?

phases.label: Check the speed
steps: Segment A: speed $= |{+4}| = 4\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Segment B: speed $= |{-4}| = 4\ \mathrm{m/s}$.
So the speed is indeed the same on both segments.

phases.label: Check the direction
steps: Segment A is at $+4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (positive direction); segment B is at $-4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (negative direction).

phases.label: Decide
steps: Constant velocity needs speed **and** direction unchanged. The direction changed, so the velocity is **not** constant from $0$ to $7\ \mathrm{s}$.
The graph shows it directly: the velocity ran from $+4$ down through $0$ to $-4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ during the $3$–$4\ \mathrm{s}$ transition.

workedExample.keyMove: Equal speeds are not enough. A reversal keeps the speed and breaks the velocity.

formativeCheck.question: A drone flies a large circle at a steady $6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (its speed never changes). Is the drone's velocity constant?
choices: Yes — the speed is unchanged, so the velocity is constant.
No — the direction is continuously changing, so the velocity is not constant even though the speed is.
Yes — flying in a circle always means constant velocity.
It cannot be decided without knowing the radius of the circle.

feedback.correct: Correct — constant velocity needs unchanged speed AND direction. Going around a circle, the direction changes at every instant, so the velocity is not constant.

incorrect.0: Unchanged speed is only half the test. The direction must also be unchanged, and on a circle it never is.
incorrect.2: Circular motion at steady speed is the classic case of *constant speed, changing velocity* — the direction turns the whole way around.
incorrect.3: The radius does not matter. Any circular path means the direction is always changing, so the velocity is never constant.

hint: Constant velocity = unchanged speed AND unchanged direction. Which one fails when you go around a circle?
formativeCheck.solution: The speed is constant, but on a circular path the direction of motion changes continuously. Because velocity includes direction, a continuously changing direction means the velocity is not constant — regardless of the radius.

chunks.title: Displacement during constant-velocity motion
chunks.concept:
When the velocity is constant over an interval, the displacement is the velocity times the elapsed time: $$\Delta x = v\,\Delta t$$ Because $v$ carries a sign, so does $\Delta x$. The elapsed time $\Delta t$ is always positive. Declare the positive direction first, substitute $v$ **with its sign**, and interpret the sign of the answer as a direction.

On a velocity-time graph, $v\,\Delta t$ is exactly the area between the horizontal segment and the time axis — a segment below the axis contributes a negative displacement.
chunks.representation:
Work in one order:

1. Declare the positive direction.
2. Write $v$ with its sign and $\Delta t$ as a positive number.
3. Multiply: $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t$.
4. State the result as a distance in a named direction.

workedExample.problem: (a) A cart moves east at a steady $3.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $6.0\ \mathrm{s}$. Take east as positive. Find its displacement. (b) A robot moves west at a steady $2.4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $7.5\ \mathrm{s}$, still with east as positive. Find its displacement.

phases.label: (a) Set up and substitute
steps: East is positive, and the cart moves east, so $v = +3.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$; $\Delta t = 6.0\ \mathrm{s}$.

phases.label: (a) Evaluate and interpret
steps: $\Delta x = +21\ \mathrm{m}$ — the cart finishes $21\ \mathrm{m}$ east of where it started.

phases.label: (b) Substitute with the sign
steps: The robot moves west, which is the negative direction here, so $v = -2.4\ \mathrm{m/s}$; $\Delta t = 7.5\ \mathrm{s}$.

phases.label: (b) Interpret
steps: The negative sign means $18\ \mathrm{m}$ in the negative direction — the robot ends $18\ \mathrm{m}$ west of its start.

workedExample.keyMove: Carry the sign of $v$ all the way through; the sign of $\Delta x$ is the direction of the trip.

formativeCheck.question: Take north as positive. A train travels south at a constant $25\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $8.0\ \mathrm{s}$. What is its displacement?
choices: $-200\ \mathrm{m}$
$+200\ \mathrm{m}$
$-3.1\ \mathrm{m}$
$+25\ \mathrm{m}$

feedback.correct: Correct — south is negative, so $v = -25\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and $\Delta x = (-25)(8.0) = -200\ \mathrm{m}$, i.e. $200\ \mathrm{m}$ south.

incorrect.1: The magnitude is right, but south is the negative direction in a north-positive frame, so the displacement must be negative.
incorrect.2: This divides instead of multiplying. $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t$ is a product.
incorrect.3: This reports the speed, not the displacement. Multiply by the $8.0\ \mathrm{s}$ interval.

hint: South is the negative direction here, so write $v = -25\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Then $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t$.
formativeCheck.solution: In a north-positive frame, travelling south means $v = -25\ \mathrm{m/s}$. $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t = (-25\ \mathrm{m/s})(8.0\ \mathrm{s}) = -200\ \mathrm{m}$ — 200 m to the south.

misconceptions.question: A velocity-time graph shows a horizontal segment at $-8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ followed by a horizontal segment at $-3\ \mathrm{m/s}$. A student says “the object sped up, because $-3$ is greater than $-8$.” What is the correct reading?
choices: The object sped up, because the velocity value increased.
The object slowed down: its speed went from $8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to $3\ \mathrm{m/s}$, both in the negative direction.
The object reversed direction between the two segments.
Nothing can be said, because both velocities are negative.

feedback.correct: Correct — speed is the size of the velocity: $|{-8}| = 8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ then $|{-3}| = 3\ \mathrm{m/s}$. The speed decreased, so the object slowed down, still moving in the negative direction.

incorrect.0: “Speeding up” is about speed, and the speed is $|v|$. From $8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to $3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ the speed dropped.
incorrect.2: Both segments are negative, so the direction did not change. A reversal would need the sign to flip.
incorrect.3: Plenty can be said: compare the speeds $|{-8}|$ and $|{-3}|$ to see the object slowed down.

hint: Speed is the magnitude of velocity — ignore the sign for “faster or slower,” then use the sign for direction.
$|-8| = 8$, $|-3| = 3$. Did the speed rise or fall?
misconceptions.solution: Both velocities are negative, so the direction is unchanged (negative direction throughout). Speed is $|v|$: it goes from $8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to $3\ \mathrm{m/s}$, a decrease. The object slowed down while continuing in the negative direction. Comparing the raw signed values ($-3 > -8$) is not how you judge speeding up or slowing down.

errorAnalysis.studentWork:
Problem: Take east as positive. A cyclist rides west at a steady $4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $12\ \mathrm{s}$. Find the displacement.

Student's response: “The cyclist moves at $4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $12\ \mathrm{s}$, so $\Delta x = (4.0)(12) = +48\ \mathrm{m}$. The displacement is $48\ \mathrm{m}$ east.”
prompts: State the rule for the sign of $v$ in $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t$.
Identify the first step that is not supported by that rule.
Repair the response: give the correct signed displacement and its direction, and check it against the declared frame.
errorAnalysis.modelResponse: The rule: $v$ is written with the sign of its direction in the declared frame; here east is positive, so motion west is $v = -4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. The first unsupported step is using $v = +4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$: the cyclist rides west, which is negative in an east-positive frame, so the student dropped the sign. Correct: $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t = (-4.0\ \mathrm{m/s})(12\ \mathrm{s}) = -48\ \mathrm{m}$, i.e. $48\ \mathrm{m}$ west. Check: a negative displacement in an east-positive frame does mean a westward finish, which matches “rides west.”

representationConnections: A verbal description gives speed and direction; the direction becomes a sign on $v$; a velocity-time graph shows that signed $v$ as a height and shows constant-vs-changing as horizontal-vs-sloped; and $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t$ (the signed area of a horizontal segment) turns a constant-velocity interval into a signed displacement. Every representation must agree on both the size and the direction.

lessonAssessment.question: A velocity-time graph has three horizontal segments: $+5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $0$–$2\ \mathrm{s}$, $+5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $2$–$6\ \mathrm{s}$, and $-5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for $6$–$10\ \mathrm{s}$. Over which interval is the velocity constant?
choices: $0$–$6\ \mathrm{s}$ only.
$0$–$10\ \mathrm{s}$ (the whole trip), because the speed is $5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ throughout.
$6$–$10\ \mathrm{s}$ only.
None of the trip, because the graph has more than one segment.

feedback.correct: Correct — from $0$ to $6\ \mathrm{s}$ the velocity holds at $+5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (same speed, same direction). At $t = 6\ \mathrm{s}$ it reverses to $-5\ \mathrm{m/s}$, so the velocity is not constant across that change.

incorrect.1: The speed is $5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ throughout, but the direction reverses at $t = 6\ \mathrm{s}$. Constant velocity needs both unchanged.
incorrect.2: The $6$–$10\ \mathrm{s}$ segment is constant velocity on its own, but so is $0$–$6\ \mathrm{s}$, and it is the longer constant-velocity interval.
incorrect.3: Multiple segments is fine — each horizontal segment is its own constant-velocity interval. The question asks for the interval where velocity holds steady, which is $0$–$6\ \mathrm{s}$.

hint: The first two segments are both $+5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ — same value, so together they are one constant-velocity interval.
At $t = 6\ \mathrm{s}$ the sign flips. Does the velocity stay constant across a sign flip?
lessonAssessment.solution: Segments $0$–$2\ \mathrm{s}$ and $2$–$6\ \mathrm{s}$ are both at $+5\ \mathrm{m/s}$, so the velocity is unchanged from $0$ to $6\ \mathrm{s}$. At $t = 6\ \mathrm{s}$ the velocity reverses to $-5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (same speed, opposite direction), which is a change in velocity. So the velocity is constant only over $0$–$6\ \mathrm{s}$.

lessonAssessment.question: A witness says: “The car had constant velocity — I watched the speedometer hold at $50\ \mathrm{km/h}$ for the whole block.” What additional information, if any, is needed to accept the claim?
choices: Nothing more is needed; a steady speedometer reading proves constant velocity.
Whether the car's direction of travel stayed the same over that block.
The exact length of the block in metres.
The car's acceleration, which must be measured directly.

feedback.correct: Correct — a steady speedometer establishes constant speed only. Constant velocity also requires an unchanged direction, so you need to know whether the car went straight or turned.

incorrect.0: The speedometer shows speed, not direction. If the car rounded a curve at $50\ \mathrm{km/h}$, its velocity was changing the whole time.
incorrect.2: The block length would let you find the displacement, but it says nothing about whether the velocity was constant.
incorrect.3: You do not need a direct acceleration measurement — knowing the direction held (together with the steady speed) is enough to confirm constant velocity.

hint: A speedometer reports speed. What is the other thing velocity depends on?
lessonAssessment.solution: Constant velocity requires unchanged speed AND unchanged direction. The witness has established constant speed only. The missing piece is whether the direction of travel stayed the same — i.e. whether the car went straight down the block or turned along it.

lessonAssessment.scenario:
Take east as positive. A delivery cart's velocity-time graph is made of three horizontal segments:

| Segment | Interval | Velocity |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $0$ s to $4$ s | $+3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ |
| 2 | $4$ s to $9$ s | $0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ |
| 3 | $9$ s to $13$ s | $-2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ |

parts.prompt: (a) Classify each of the three segments as constant velocity or changing velocity, and describe the motion each represents in words (include direction).
parts.modelResponse: All three segments are horizontal, so each is a constant-velocity interval. Segment 1: moving east at $3\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Segment 2: at rest ($v = 0$). Segment 3: moving west at $2\ \mathrm{m/s}$. (The velocity is *not* constant across the whole trip, because it changes between segments.)

parts.prompt: (b) Calculate the cart's displacement during each segment using $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t$, keeping signs.
parts.modelResponse: Segment 1: $\Delta x_1 = (+3\ \mathrm{m/s})(4\ \mathrm{s}) = +12\ \mathrm{m}$. Segment 2: $\Delta x_2 = (0)(5\ \mathrm{s}) = 0\ \mathrm{m}$. Segment 3: $\Delta x_3 = (-2\ \mathrm{m/s})(4\ \mathrm{s}) = -8\ \mathrm{m}$.

parts.prompt: (c) Find the cart's total displacement from $t = 0$ to $t = 13\ \mathrm{s}$, and state its direction.
parts.modelResponse: Add the signed segment displacements: $\Delta x = (+12) + 0 + (-8) = +4\ \mathrm{m}$. The cart finishes $4\ \mathrm{m}$ east of where it started.

parts.prompt: (d) A student claims segment 3 shows the cart “speeding up from rest” because it comes right after the cart was stopped. Explain what is wrong with this claim.
parts.modelResponse: Segment 3 is horizontal at $-2\ \mathrm{m/s}$, so the velocity is constant during it — the cart is not speeding up at all within the segment; it moves west at a steady $2\ \mathrm{m/s}$. The change from rest to $-2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ happens at the boundary at $t = 9\ \mathrm{s}$, not across segment 3. Also “speeding up” describes an increasing speed over time, which a horizontal segment never shows.

examConnection: Signed velocity, the speed-vs-velocity distinction, and $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t$ (as an area) are the foundation for velocity-time graph slope and area work in the next lesson and for choosing kinematics equations later. AP and IB Paper 1 routinely test whether a described or graphed motion is constant-velocity and whether a negative value means “backward” or “slowing.”
summary: Velocity is signed: the sign is direction, and speed is its magnitude. On a velocity-time graph, a horizontal segment is constant velocity and a sloped segment is changing velocity; a negative value means the negative direction, not “slowing down.” Velocity is constant only when speed AND direction are both unchanged — a reversal (or a turn) keeps the speed but changes the velocity. For a constant-velocity interval, $\Delta x = v\,\Delta t$, carrying the sign of $v$; this is the area between the segment and the time axis.

exitQuestion.question: An object moves in a straight line and never changes direction. Its speed is $6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at the start and $6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at the end of a $10\ \mathrm{s}$ interval. Can you conclude its velocity was constant for the whole interval?
choices: Yes — same speed at both ends and no direction change means constant velocity.
No — the speed could have risen and fallen again in between, so the velocity need not have been constant throughout.
Yes — a straight-line path always means constant velocity.
No — constant velocity is impossible over a $10\ \mathrm{s}$ interval.

feedback.correct: Correct — matching the speed only at the two ends does not rule out changes in between. The velocity is constant only if the speed held at $6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ the entire time.

incorrect.0: Equal speeds at the endpoints do not guarantee equal speed throughout — the object could have sped up and slowed back down.
incorrect.2: A straight path fixes the direction but not the speed. The speed could still vary along the line.
incorrect.3: Constant velocity over $10\ \mathrm{s}$ is entirely possible; the point is that the given information does not confirm it.

hint: You are told the speed at the start and the end only. What might it have done in between?
exitQuestion.solution: The direction is fixed (straight line, no reversal), so that box is checked. But the speed is only known at the two endpoints; it could have increased and then decreased back to $6\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Without knowing the speed held constant for the whole interval, you cannot conclude the velocity was constant throughout.
